segments.sourceText: Look up on a clear day, and the sky is blue. But sunlight itself is white. So where does the blue come from?
segments.candidateSpokenText: Look up on a clear day. The sky is blue. But sunlight itself? White. So where does the blue actually come from?
segments.changeNotes: hook tightened into short spoken breath groups; question kept as the hook

segments.sourceText: The answer is written in the air itself. Tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far smaller than a wave of light.
segments.candidateSpokenText: The answer is written into the air itself — tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, each one far smaller than a wave of light.
segments.changeNotes: dash cadence; 'each one' clarifies the antecedent without changing the comparison

segments.sourceText: When sunlight hits them, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction, several times more strongly than red.
segments.candidateSpokenText: When sunlight hits those molecules, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction — several times more strongly than they scatter red.
segments.changeNotes: comparison phrase 'several times more strongly than' preserved verbatim

segments.sourceText: That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. That is why the whole sky glows blue.
segments.candidateSpokenText: That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. And that is why the whole sky glows blue.

segments.sourceText: Violet is scattered even more, but there is less of it in sunlight, and your eyes are less sensitive to it.
segments.candidateSpokenText: Violet gets scattered even more. But there is less of it in sunlight to begin with, and your eyes are less sensitive to it.
segments.changeNotes: split into two breath groups; both qualifiers preserved

segments.sourceText: At sunset, sunlight crosses much more air. The blue is scattered away, and the reds and oranges remain.
segments.candidateSpokenText: At sunset, that sunlight crosses much more air. The blue gets scattered away along the way, and the reds and oranges remain.
segments.changeNotes: 'much more air' preserved; added journey phrasing for spoken flow

segments.sourceText: Dust and pollution scatter all colors equally, which is why a hazy sky looks pale and white.
segments.candidateSpokenText: Dust and pollution, on the other hand, scatter all colors equally. That is why a hazy sky looks pale and white.

segments.sourceText: So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.
segments.candidateSpokenText: So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.

changeSummary: Bounded spoken-cadence rewrite: sentence splits, spoken transitions, rhythm; all facts/qualifiers/comparisons preserved; closing beat unchanged.
